# Introduction

`redstone` is a from-scratch, C99 reimplementation of the `sqlite3(1)` command-line
shell. It is built to be a **drop-in replacement**: every dot command, output
mode, and command-line flag that upstream `sqlite3(1)` accepts is either
implemented to the same behaviour or refused with an explicit message — never
silently ignored. `redstone --compat` reproduces upstream exactly, verified
byte-for-byte by a differential test suite that runs the same input through
both binaries and compares the output.

Outside `--compat`, redstone adds what a modern interactive shell is expected to
have and upstream's `shell.c` does not: a navigable, zsh-style completion
menu; live syntax highlighting of the statement as it is typed; a colour theme
system; and box-drawn, terminal-width-aware output by default. The design
premise is that `alias sqlite3=redstone` should survive a normal day's work —
nothing about scripting or automation should notice the substitution, while
interactive use gets meaningfully better.

This document explains what the program does, how it is built internally, and
why its structure looks the way it does. It draws together the project's
architecture notes, its development methodology, its manual testing guide,
and its reference manual into one continuous account, for a reader meeting
the codebase for the first time.

## Scope and non-goals

Stating what `redstone` deliberately does not attempt keeps the rest of the
design legible:

- **No bundled SQLite extensions.** Upstream `shell.c` carries `sqlar`,
  `zipfile`, `sha3`, `sqlite3expert`, `sqlite3recover`, `sqlite3_intck`,
  `sqlite3session`, and `dbdata` — together the bulk of its 37,000-plus lines.
  The dot commands that depend on them are recognised and refused with a
  message naming the missing extension, so the gap is documented rather than
  silently discovered at the worst moment.
- **No SQL parser.** Completion needs to know *where the cursor is* inside a
  statement, not what the statement means. A tokenizer and a cursor-context
  state machine are sufficient; a full parser would be scope the feature does
  not need.
- **No Windows support.** POSIX termios is assumed throughout the terminal
  layer.

# Why a clean-room reimplementation

The upstream client, `shell.c`, is 37,373 lines and over a megabyte in the
pinned SQLite 3.53.3 — machine-generated by concatenating `src/shell.c.in`
with a dozen extension sources. It cannot be meaningfully diffed, re-derived,
or hand-maintained, and grafting a completion engine onto it would mean
owning a blob nobody in this project wrote.

`redstone` is therefore built against the public `sqlite3` C API rather than as a
textual fork. Upstream `shell.c` is kept for consultation only: `make
reference` copies it into `reference/`, sourced from the same amalgamation
the Nix flake already pins — so the project names one SQLite version, not two
— and the copy is excluded from git. When an upstream behaviour must be
matched exactly (a quoting rule, a dot command's flag set, the precise
column-width algorithm), it is read there and reimplemented deliberately.

The tradeoff this accepts is that parity must be *built and verified*
deliberately rather than inherited for free. It is measured, not claimed: the
gate runs a differential suite that executes identical input through `redstone
--compat` and the `sqlite3` binary from the flake and diffs the two outputs
byte for byte. What is gained in return is that every line under `src/` is
the project's own, small, and auditable.

## Dependencies

`redstone` depends on exactly one library beyond libc and POSIX: `libsqlite3`.

Notably absent is any line-editing library. This is a deliberate consequence
of the feature set, not asceticism: GNU readline, libedit, and linenoise all
implement completion as *print a list of candidates and return to the
prompt*. None has a concept of a persistent, navigable selection menu that
narrows as the user keeps typing. Reproducing zsh's completion behaviour means
owning the terminal outright, so `redstone` does, in `line.c` and `menu.c`.

Two build paths exist for SQLite itself, and both are exercised by the gate:

- `make` links the system `libsqlite3`, located by `pkg-config`. Because the
  Nix flake pins nixpkgs, this path is reproducible across machines.
- `make SQLITE=vendored` compiles the SQLite amalgamation directly, producing
  a binary with no external SQLite dependency at all. The amalgamation itself
  is fetched by the flake and never committed — 9.4 MB and roughly 266,000
  lines — and the flake's pinned amalgamation version is kept equal to
  `pkgs.sqlite`'s, with the dev shell warning if they drift apart.

Build objects land in `build/<backend>/<mode>/`, and the directory is keyed on
both dimensions deliberately: a single shared `build/` tree lets `make test`
link objects an earlier `make debug` compiled without sanitizers, which would
let the suite pass while running uninstrumented — keying by mode closes that
hole.

# Module decomposition

Each module is one `.c` file in `src/` with a matching header in `include/`.
Each owns exactly one concern and depends only on the modules below it in the
stack; no module reaches into another's internals.

```
main.c      argument parsing (upstream flag set) and nothing else
  |
  +-- shell.c   the session: the current connection and the auxiliary ones,
  |     |       the .output/.once redirect, the switches, statement
  |     |       execution, the REPL, the init files
  |     |
  |     +-- dot.c     the command table and dispatch: 76 rows,
  |     |             64 implemented and 12 refused
  |     +-- schema.c  .schema .fullschema .dump .databases .indexes .tables
  |     |             .dbinfo .dbtotxt .clone .lint -- byte-exact ports
  |     +-- import.c  .import (RFC 4180 CSV and ASCII-delimited), .excel/.www
  |     |
  |     +-- out.c    the 22 output-mode presets, box drawing, type-aware colour
  |           |
  |           +-- width.c   UTF-8 display width, also used by menu.c
  |
  +-- line.c    raw-mode line editor: keys, cursor, history, redraw
  |     |
  |     +-- hl.c      syntax highlighting of the buffer being typed
  |     +-- menu.c    completion menu: layout, navigation, rendering
  |           |
  |           +-- comp.c    candidate generation: asks sqlctx where we are,
  |                 |       asks db what exists, returns a candidate list
  |                 +-- sqlctx.c   SQL tokenizer + cursor-context state machine
  |
  +-- theme.c   colour table, terminal capability detection, theme file
  +-- db.c      sqlite3 handle, statement execution, schema introspection,
                the value cache
```

Two placements in this diagram encode load-bearing decisions rather than
convenience.

First, `out.c` sits **under** `db.c`, not above it. `db.c` hands the
formatter typed values and column names and decides nothing about
appearance, and nothing above `db.c` includes `<sqlite3.h>` at all. That
separation is what lets the formatter be unit-tested against synthetic rows
with no database attached, and it is also what lets the differential parity
suite treat the entire pipeline, from query text to output bytes, as a single
pure function.

Second, `sqlctx.c` and `comp.c` are pure with respect to the terminal: each
takes a buffer and a cursor offset and returns data, touching no global
state and no I/O. That purity is what makes the completion engine
unit-testable without a pseudo-terminal, and it is the main reason the module
boundaries were drawn where they were.

## Connection settings and correctness

`db.c` applies upstream's connection settings itself, both on first open and
on every `.open`: double-quoted string literals off for DDL and DML,
defensive mode on, trusted-schema off, statement scan-status off, extension
loading enabled. These are behavioural choices, not decoration — with
double-quoted-string-literals off, `SELECT "typo"` is a compile error rather
than a string literal that silently returns the wrong thing.

Disabling that setting explicitly matters because upstream `sqlite3(1)`
compiles its own SQLite with `-DSQLITE_DQS=0`, while `redstone` links whichever
shared `libsqlite3` the system provides, which may or may not have been built
the same way. Setting it in `db.c` makes the two shells behave identically
regardless of which library sits underneath either one.

## No globals below `main.c`

A dot command is handed a `Shell` struct and reaches everything else through
it — there is no global mutable state anywhere below `main.c`. The redirect a
command writes to, for instance, is always `shell_out(sh)`: the `.output`
file while one is active, the base stream otherwise. This is also why
`.once` needs no special-casing in the REPL loop — the shell simply ends the
redirect after the next statement runs.

# The completion pipeline

A `<Tab>` keystroke at cursor offset $n$ in buffer $b$ flows through three
stages.

## Stage 1: context analysis

`sqlctx_analyze(b, n)` tokenizes the buffer — respecting string literals,
`--` and `/* */` comments, and quoted identifiers (`"x"`, `` `x` ``, `[x]`) —
then walks the resulting token stream to produce a context structure:

```c
typedef struct {
    SqlCtxKind kind;       /* what may appear here */
    const char *prefix;    /* the partial word under the cursor */
    size_t      prefix_len;
    TableRef    tables[SQLCTX_MAX_TABLES];  /* from FROM/JOIN, with aliases */
    size_t      table_count;
    char        column[SQLCTX_MAX_IDENT];   /* for VALUE contexts */
} SqlContext;
```

`kind` takes one of nine values: `CTX_DOT_COMMAND`, `CTX_DOT_ARG`,
`CTX_STATEMENT_START`, `CTX_SELECT_LIST`, `CTX_TABLE`, `CTX_COLUMN`,
`CTX_VALUE`, `CTX_KEYWORD`, or `CTX_UNKNOWN`.

## Stage 2: candidate generation

`comp_candidates(ctx, db)` maps that context to a source of candidates:

| Context | Candidates |
|---|---|
| `CTX_DOT_COMMAND` | the dot-command table in `dot.c` |
| `CTX_DOT_ARG` | per-command: table names, modes, filenames |
| `CTX_STATEMENT_START` | statement keywords (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, …) |
| `CTX_SELECT_LIST` | columns of tables already named in `FROM`; else all |
| `CTX_TABLE` | tables and views |
| `CTX_COLUMN` | columns scoped to the `FROM` set, alias-qualified |
| `CTX_VALUE` | distinct values of the column being compared |
| `CTX_KEYWORD` | keywords valid after the preceding token |

Scoping is the entire point of this stage: `SELECT * FROM companies WHERE
<Tab>` must offer the seven columns that belong to `companies`, not every
column in the database. Table-scoped completion is what separates this from
a naive identifier-matching completer.

## Stage 3: menu presentation

`menu_show(candidates)` renders the candidate list below the prompt and takes
over input handling. `Tab`, `→`, and `Ctrl-N` move to the next candidate;
`Shift-Tab`, `←`, and `Ctrl-P` move to the previous one; `Enter` accepts the
selection; `Esc` or `Ctrl-G` dismisses the menu. Typing while the menu is
open narrows the candidate list in place rather than closing it — matching
the zsh behaviour the feature is modeled on. A context with exactly one
candidate is inserted directly, with no menu drawn at all.

## Value completion

`CTX_VALUE` is the only context that reads user data rather than schema
metadata, so it is deliberately bounded on every axis:

- The underlying query is `SELECT DISTINCT <col> FROM <tbl> LIMIT 200`, with
  identifiers quoted.
- A `sqlite3_progress_handler` callback aborts the query after roughly 150 ms,
  producing no menu rather than a stalled prompt.
- Results are cached per `(table, column)` pair for the session, and the
  cache is invalidated whenever a statement that modifies the database runs.
- When the 200-row cap is hit, the menu says so explicitly, so a truncated
  list is never mistaken for a complete one.

Value completion is on by default; `.complete values off` disables it for
sessions against databases where even a capped scan is unwelcome.

# Highlighting and theming

`hl_write(out, text, from, to, schema)` writes a window of the line currently
being typed, coloured token by token. It reuses `sqlctx.c`'s lexer rather
than maintaining a second one — two independent lexers would eventually
drift, and highlighting would stop agreeing with completion about what a
token is. `hl_write` always analyses the *whole* line, even when only part of
it is being redrawn, because a string literal that opened before the visible
window still needs to colour everything after it correctly.

`hl.c` itself knows nothing about a database; schema knowledge arrives
through four callbacks:

```c
typedef struct {
    bool (*is_keyword)(void *ctx, const char *name, size_t len);
    bool (*is_function)(void *ctx, const char *name, size_t len);
    bool (*is_table)(void *ctx, const char *name, size_t len, bool *is_view);
    bool (*is_column)(void *ctx, const char *name, size_t len,
                      const SqlCtxTable *tables, size_t ntables);
    void *ctx;
} HlSchema;
```

`main.c` supplies the concrete callbacks; `line.c` merely carries the
struct through — the same injection pattern used for the completer, and for
the same reason: nothing above `db.c` may include `<sqlite3.h>`, and every
colouring decision becomes independently testable against a stub
implementation. Each callback is asked once per identifier per keystroke and
never queries the database directly — it answers from a cache `db.c` already
maintains and invalidates on the schema cookie. Columns are looked up only
within the tables that `sqlctx_analyze` reports for the current statement,
which is why `SELECT id` leaves `id` in the plain foreground while `SELECT id
FROM users` colours it as a known column.

The payoff of this design is direct: a name the database does not recognise
stays in the terminal's plain foreground colour, making a typo visible before
the statement is ever executed.

## The theme system

Nothing in the program hardcodes a colour. `theme.c` holds exactly one SGR
(ANSI Select Graphic Rendition) escape string per style, and the four
built-in palettes — `default`, `dark`, `light`, and the 16-colour-safe
`basic` — exist as theme-file *text* compiled into the binary, parsed by the
same code path a user-supplied theme file goes through. There is therefore
nothing a shipped theme can do that a user's theme file cannot also do, and
nothing to install separately.

A theme file is an INI-style document: `[menu]`, `[syntax]`, and `[output]`
sections containing `key = value` lines, where a value is zero or more text
attributes plus at most one foreground and one background colour — for
example `bold blue`, `dim`, `underline #ff0080 on 52`, or `none`. A line whose
first non-blank character is `#` is a comment, and `--` comments to end of
line as in SQL; `#` cannot serve double duty as a SQL-style comment marker,
because a value is the one place a `#rrggbb` colour literal legitimately
appears. Unknown sections, keys, or values are reported and skipped
individually — a typo in a theme file costs the user that one line, never the
whole palette and never the shell's ability to start.

`theme_dump` writes the live, in-memory palette back out in exactly this
format, so `.theme` with no argument is simultaneously a listing and a
ready-to-edit starting point; a test asserts the round trip for every shipped
palette. `.theme` also accepts `list`, `reload`, `on`/`off`, a built-in name,
or a file path. The theme file itself lives at `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/redstone/theme`
(defaulting to `~/.config/redstone/theme`), and `-noinit` suppresses it exactly
as it suppresses `~/.sqliterc`.

# Terminal handling

`line.c` places the terminal into raw mode with `tcsetattr`, and restores it
both from an `atexit` handler and from `SIGINT`, `SIGTERM`, `SIGQUIT`, and
`SIGHUP` handlers — a shell that leaves a user's terminal stuck in raw mode
after a crash is a worse outcome than crashing with a clean terminal.
`SIGWINCH` triggers a re-layout of any open completion menu, so a resized
window does not leave stale rows on screen.

Output uses plain ANSI escape sequences directly; there is no dependency on
terminfo or ncurses. The escape set in use is small and universally
supported: cursor movement, erase-line, erase-to-end-of-screen, and SGR
colour codes. When standard output is not a terminal, `redstone` reads lines
with `fgets` and performs no editing at all, so piping input through the
shell continues to work exactly as it would with any other batch tool.

Two edge cases are tracked deliberately rather than papered over: input
lines longer than the terminal's width, and multi-line statement
continuation. UTF-8 display width — needed for both of these, and for
aligning box-drawn output around wide or combining characters — has its own
module, `width.c`, shared between the output formatter and the completion
menu.

# Error handling conventions

The codebase follows a small, consistent set of rules for failure paths:

- Functions that can fail return `bool` or a negative `int` — never a
  sentinel pointer value the caller is expected to compare against something
  magic.
- Allocation failure is reported upward to the caller, never treated as
  fatal, except inside `main` itself.
- Every `sqlite3_stmt` is finalized on every code path, including error
  paths — there is no path that leaks a prepared statement.
- No global mutable state exists outside `main.c`'s single `Shell` struct,
  which every function that needs it receives explicitly as a parameter.

# Output modes and parity

The default output mode, whether the session is interactive or not, is
`box`: headers on, colour on, sized to the real terminal width via
`ioctl(TIOCGWINSZ)`, re-read before every result so that resizing the window
takes effect starting with the next query. `--compat` switches the default
to `list`, headers off, no colour — upstream's own default.

Thirteen "classic" output modes (`ascii box column csv html insert json line
list markdown quote table tabs`) are byte-parity-tested against `sqlite3(1)`
by `make parity`; nine further modes (`c count jatom jobject off psql qbox
split tcl`) are best-effort, since they either have no clean upstream
equivalent to diff against or are rarely used enough that hand verification
suffices. Inside the shell, `.help mode` lists the option flags each mode
accepts.

Where `redstone` knowingly diverges from upstream — an extension this build does
not vendor, or an output mode the shipped `sqlite3(1)` binary itself
rejects — the gap is refused loudly, with an error naming exactly what is
missing, rather than approximated silently. `docs/notes/` and the project's
internal roadmap carry the complete, current list of such gaps; inside the
running shell, `.help` marks each of the eleven currently-refused dot
commands as such.

# Development methodology

The project follows a specification-driven workflow designed for an
autonomous coding agent working under human supervision, structured around a
small number of principles.

**Ground truth lives on disk, never only in conversation.** A project
tracking file is authoritative, and its roadmap checkboxes are the state of
record; a fresh working context — after a restart, a new session, or handing
work to a sub-agent — resumes from nothing but "execute phase *N*" plus that
file.

**Planning is supervised; implementation is autonomous.** Design decisions
are resolved with the project owner at planning time and recorded in the
roadmap. Execution then proceeds one phase per fresh context, without a human
in the loop, except at the manual-check gate described below.

**An undefined decision is flagged, never guessed.** If a phase's plan is
silent on a question that implementation needs answered, that is a stop
condition, not an invitation to improvise.

**Nothing is tracked outside the roadmap.** Work discovered mid-phase — a bug,
a missing edge case, a deferred improvement — is recorded in the roadmap
itself, as a task, a deferred-work entry, or a new phase; it is never carried
only in conversation or left implicit.

## The gate

Every phase is certified by one command producing one of three verdicts:
PASS, FAIL, or BLOCKED. The gate, not any agent's self-assessment, is the
sole arbiter of whether a phase is done.

A green result requires, simultaneously:

- a clean formatter run,
- a clean linter run,
- a clean type/compiler check,
- **zero warnings** across the build and every check above — a warning is
  treated as a defect, fixed at its cause or explicitly waived in the
  roadmap with a written rationale, never suppressed silently or globally,
  and
- at least one acceptance test that actually **passed**, not merely
  collected or skipped — a skipped test does not count as a pass.

Concretely, in this repository, `make gate` runs the formatter, both the
debug and release builds under `-Werror`, the ASan/UBSan-instrumented test
suite, the differential parity suite, `cppcheck`, and `clang-tidy`, in that
order, stopping at the first failure.

## The manual-check gate

Some behaviour cannot be honestly verified by an automatic check: visual
menu placement, whether colours read legibly on a real terminal, whether a
resize behaves correctly on real hardware. Any phase that carries such a
manual check is completed up through a green automatic gate, has its roadmap
entry marked in-progress, and then **halts** — the agent does not commit.
The project owner performs the listed manual checks and confirms them; only
then are the phase's checkboxes marked done and the commit made. A green
automatic gate is explicitly not, by itself, authority to commit a phase with
outstanding manual checks.

## Version control conventions

Git tracks every change. One commit corresponds to one phase, made only once
that phase's gate is green and any manual checks it carries have been
confirmed by the owner. Commit messages follow a fixed convention — a prefix
naming the affected area, a concise imperative summary, and a body explaining
what changed and why whenever the summary alone is not enough. Paths are
staged explicitly; nothing is ever staged with a blanket `add -A`. Nothing is
ever pushed, and no release tag is ever cut, without an explicit instruction
from the owner.

# Manual verification

Automatic tests cannot fully exercise the terminal layer, since several
behaviours — real window resizing, real terminal-emulator rendering
quirks, and subjective legibility — depend on a live controlling terminal
that a test harness cannot faithfully simulate. The project keeps a
dedicated manual testing guide for this reason, organized by the same module
boundaries as the architecture itself, so a change to one module points
directly at the section of manual checks it should also motivate:

| Area changed | Manual checks to run |
|---|---|
| `out.c`, `width.c` | Output modes, screen width, CJK/combining-character alignment |
| `menu.c`, `comp.c`, `sqlctx.c` | Completion menu behaviour |
| `hl.c`, `theme.c` | Syntax highlighting, theme loading and legibility |
| `edit.c`, `line.c` | Line editor, keybindings, pty-driven behaviour |
| `dot.c`, `schema.c`, `import.c`, `shell.c`, `main.c` | Dot-command and CLI parity, plus `make parity` |

Representative checks from that guide illustrate the kind of behaviour being
protected: that a completion menu narrows in place rather than closing when
the user keeps typing; that `Esc` restores the input buffer to exactly its
pre-`Tab` state; that an unknown column name in a `SELECT` list is left in
the plain foreground rather than falsely highlighted as known; that
`-screenwidth 1` is rejected with a specific exit code rather than silently
clamped; and that killing the shell mid-line with `SIGTERM` leaves the
terminal in normal, non-raw mode without requiring the user to run `reset`.

# Using redstone

## Building

The entire toolchain is pinned by a Nix flake; no system dependency beyond
`libsqlite3` is assumed.

```sh
nix develop            # enter the dev shell once, then run make from inside it
make                    # debug build -> bin/redstone
make release            # optimised build
make SQLITE=vendored    # build against the SQLite amalgamation instead
make test               # unit + pty tests under ASan+UBSan
make parity             # differential output test vs the real sqlite3(1)
make gate               # format, both builds, tests, parity, cppcheck, clang-tidy
make install PREFIX=~/.local
```

`make help` lists every target, including `valgrind`, `fuzz`, `tidy`,
`cppcheck`, `compdb`, and `watch`. Without Nix, `nix build` — using the
flake's default package — produces the same release binary.

`make install` places `bin/redstone` and its man page only; it never installs a
symlink or copy named `sqlite3`, leaving that substitution to the user's own
`alias`.

## Basic usage

```sh
redstone mydb.db                              # interactive, completion + highlighting + box output
redstone --compat mydb.db "SELECT * FROM t;"  # scripting, byte-identical to sqlite3(1)
alias sqlite3=redstone                        # meant to survive a normal day's work
```

With no database argument, `redstone` opens an in-memory database, exactly as
`sqlite3(1)` does. Any SQL given on the command line after the database name
runs as a batch, after which the shell exits; with none given, it opens the
interactive prompt, or reads statements from standard input when that is not
a terminal.

## Keybindings

Two keymaps are available, switched at runtime with `.editor emacs` or
`.editor vi` — no restart required. Emacs is the default.

**Emacs keymap** (always available)

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `←` `→` / `Ctrl-B` `Ctrl-F` | Move the cursor one character |
| `Ctrl-A` / `Ctrl-E` | Jump to start / end of line |
| `Ctrl-W` | Delete the word before the cursor |
| `Ctrl-U` | Delete to the start of the line |
| `Ctrl-K` | Delete to the end of the line |
| `Ctrl-T` | Transpose the two characters before the cursor |
| `↑` `↓` | Walk history |
| `Ctrl-L` | Clear the screen and repaint |
| `Ctrl-C` | Abandon the current line |
| `Ctrl-D` | End of file on an empty line, delete-forward otherwise |
| `Tab` | Open (or narrow) the completion menu; accept a unique match with no menu |

**Vi keymap** (`.editor vi`), normal mode

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `h` `j` `k` `l` | Move / history |
| `0` `$` `^` | Start, end, first non-blank of the line |
| `w` `b` `e` | Word motions |
| `i` `a` `I` `A` | Enter insert mode (before/after cursor, start/end of line) |
| `x` | Delete character under the cursor |
| `d` + motion (`dw`, `dd`, ...) | Delete |
| `c` + motion (`cw`, `cc`, ...) | Change |
| `r` | Replace one character |
| `u` | Undo |
| a leading count | Repeats the motion or command |

**Completion menu**, once open (either keymap)

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `Tab` / `Shift-Tab` | Next / previous candidate |
| `←` `→` `↑` `↓`, `Ctrl-N` `Ctrl-P` | Move the selection |
| Typing | Narrows the candidates in place |
| `Enter` | Accept the selection |
| `Esc` / `Ctrl-G` | Dismiss, restoring the buffer exactly |

## Reference documentation

`man redstone` (`docs/redstone.1`) is the exhaustive reference: every flag, every
output mode, every file location, every environment variable, and the exit
status convention. It documents, among other things:

- `-safe` together with `-nonce STRING`, for running an untrusted script
  while refusing commands capable of damage outside the database file, with
  a nonce-prefixed escape hatch for individual trusted lines;
- `-screenwidth N` (minimum 2) to fix the width used for columnar output,
  overriding live terminal-width detection;
- the three-tier exit status convention: `0` on a clean exit, `1` on a SQL
  error under `-bail` or in the default non-interactive stop-on-error
  behaviour, `2` on a command-line usage error.

# Summary

`redstone` demonstrates that a drop-in-compatible tool and a meaningfully better
interactive tool are not in tension, provided compatibility is architecturally
isolated rather than bolted on. The `--compat` flag and its differential test
suite give upstream behaviour a hard boundary; everything on the other side
of that boundary — the completion pipeline, the highlighter, the theme
system — is free to diverge in whatever direction makes daily interactive use
better, because nothing about it can leak into scripted behaviour by
accident. The module layering that keeps `<sqlite3.h>` out of everything
above `db.c` is what makes both halves of that claim independently testable,
and the specification-driven workflow around the codebase is what keeps the
architecture and the roadmap from drifting apart as the project grows.
